title: Love's example
hook: Abelard stressed the cross as love so great it changes us

segments.voice: Yesterday, substitution: Barabbas walking free while another went to the cross. Your line was in my place. What burden did you take for someone? Day one thousand eighty-five.

A Roman officer is on duty at an execution. The Gospels don't say what he expected. But this death goes differently. Luke says that from the cross Jesus prays for the people killing him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." And when it's over, the officer, a centurion, says something nobody ordered him to say. Luke records it: "Certainly this was a righteous man." Nothing was paid to him. No argument convinced him. He watched how someone loved, all the way to the end, and Luke says he glorified God. Today's word: moral influence.

Moral influence is the name later writers gave to a picture stressed by Peter Abelard, a teacher in medieval Paris. The last few days asked what the cross does to death, or to a debt, or to a penalty. Abelard asked what it does to us. His answer, in a commentary on Paul's letter to the Romans: the cross is God's love shown so plainly that it wins our love in return, and that love sets us free. He leaned on a verse from that letter: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Commendeth means shows, puts on display. Not after we cleaned up. While we were yet sinners. Love goes first, and in this picture, love answers. Jesus himself said, in John's Gospel, "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." In this picture, the cross is that greater love, and seeing it changes the one who sees. People argued with Abelard in his own day. Bernard of Clairvaux worried this made the cross only an example, a beautiful one, but no rescue. Some readers of Abelard point out that he spoke of more than example, and that he called this love a real power that frees. Churches can keep this note inside their other pictures: whatever else the cross does, it shows love. The centurion's line is this picture in a single sentence: he watched, and he spoke.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE CROSS DO TO US?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let love change one reaction. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who reliably sets you off. The coworker, the relative, the driver who's always too close. Picture the moment it usually happens. Now, before the usual reaction, picture being loved first, while you were still at your worst. Let that sit a moment. Then choose one small different response for next time: a pause, a softer word, a question instead of a verdict. If you pray, you can ask for that love. The bell holds the time.
Moral influence. The picture of the cross as love shown so plainly that it wins our love and changes us, stressed by Abelard.
Your line: love that changes us. When that person sets you off today, try the different response once, and watch what turns. Day one thousand eighty-five.

howItsDone: Some Christians meditate on the cross as a sign of God's love, for example in Good Friday services, hymns about the cross, and the Stations of the Cross, letting what they see shape how they treat others.

notes: 'Moral influence' as a label is later than Abelard; the script says 'the name later writers gave'. Confirm.
Abelard's view paraphrased from his Romans commentary (the 'quaestio' on Romans 3:26): love kindled in us by the cross frees us from slavery to sin. Confirm the paraphrase.
Bernard's objection (Letter 190 / Tractatus de erroribus Abaelardi) summarized as 'only an example'. Confirm.
The centurion's change is a reading of Luke 23:47; Mark 15:39 and Matthew 27:54 give 'Son of God'. Luke chosen; not combined.
Original συνίστησιν: confirm form and pronunciation.

Editor pass: cut 1 John 4:19 ('we love him, because he first loved us'), already quoted and matched on day 1079, and its screen head (now 'greater love hath no man'); fixed the hook's ambiguous 'this man prays' to 'Jesus prays'; cut the guessed 'work shift'; 'readers of Abelard' softened to 'some readers'.
Audit pass (2026-10-02): the hook, teach and fork reveal had asserted that the centurion inwardly 'changed'; Luke 23:47 says only that he glorified God and spoke. Wording now stays with the text.
